query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A surface aluminizing treatment applied to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will form a thin, adherent Al2O3 layer that acts as a diffusion barrier against oxygen, thereby enhancing its oxidation resistance at high temperatures without degrading its inherent mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths ranging from 163 to 530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)
generation.intervention: Apply a surface aluminizing treatment (for example, via pack cementation) to deposit an Al-rich coating on the as-cast alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under low strain rate conditions analogous to those used in high-temperature mechanical evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 (alumina) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The aluminizing treatment introduces enough aluminum such that, upon high-temperature exposure in air, it preferentially oxidizes to form a stable Al2O3 layer. This protective scale slows down further oxygen ingress and mitigates pesting without altering the bulk microstructure responsible for the alloy’s beneficial mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated material, the aluminized alloy will show significantly reduced oxidation (evidenced by a thinner, more stable oxide layer) while maintaining similar room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits rapid oxidation (pesting) under air exposure at 800 °C, which degrades its mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the aluminizing treatment is expected to hold for high-temperature exposures around 800 °C for durations up to 5 hours. Its performance may be limited if the coating becomes too thick, loses adherence, or is mechanically compromised under conditions outside these boundaries (e.g., higher strain rates or repeated thermal cycling).
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how the long-term cyclic exposure and thermal-mechanical fatigue might affect the integrity of the Al2O3 layer and if the coating process might introduce microstructural defects impacting mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with the surface aluminizing treatment and one set as untreated controls. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under identical strain rate conditions. After exposure, perform detailed surface characterization and mechanical testing.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and composition (using SEM/EDS and XRD) to confirm the formation and integrity of the Al2O3 layer.
Residual room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength to compare mechanical performance of treated vs. untreated samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized samples do not exhibit a significantly thinner, more stable oxide layer or if the post-exposure mechanical properties are degraded compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
